BACKGROUND: World Trade Center (WTC)-exposed Fire Department of the City of New York (FDNY) rescue/recovery workers have an elevated risk of smoking-related morbidity. Despite access to free tobacco cessation treatment, some individuals in this population continue to smoke. In other settings, opt-out treatment approaches increase treatment initiation, but effectiveness in occupational health programs is unclear. Accordingly, we (1) assessed whether an opt-out strategy increases engagement with a Tobacco Cessation Program and (2) identified factors associated with engagement. METHODS: This was a randomized trial among FDNY firefighters and Emergency Medical Service (EMS) who self-reported smoking and were eligible for the WTC Health Program Lung Cancer Screening Program. 1:1 randomization occurred prior to contact for opt-out recruitment with Enhanced Care treatment (Opt-Out/Enhanced) or opt-in recruitment with Standard Care treatment (Opt-In/Standard). Opt-Out/Enhanced included proactive outreach and tailored biofeedback during counseling; Opt-In/Standard included participant-initiated engagement and standard counseling. Both groups were offered identical no-cost pharmacotherapy (varenicline). Engagement was defined as: consented enrollment (expressed interest and provided informed consent) and treatment initiation (attendance at ≥1 counseling session). Engagement differences were evaluated using logistic regression; sociodemographic and health-related factors were characterized descriptively without formal testing due to small numbers. RESULTS: Overall, 312 individuals were randomized (Opt-Out/Enhanced, n = 156 and Opt-In/Standard, n = 156). Engagement was low (7.4%). Consented enrollment (n = 23; OR = 3.05; 95% CI = 1.11-9.72) and treatment initiation (n = 18; OR = 2.08; 95% CI = 0.72-6.73) were higher in Opt-Out/Enhanced versus Opt-In/Standard. Treatment initiators had a median age of 60.5 (vs 65.0 years among non-initiators); 38.9% were EMS (vs 18.0%), 22.2% were female (vs 6.9%), 77.8% had a prior cessation attempt (vs 23.5%), and 55.6% had abnormal lung function (vs 32.9%). Participants were too few to analyze cessation outcomes in depth. CONCLUSIONS: Despite low engagement overall, opt-out treatment had higher engagement with tobacco cessation treatment. This supports other work that has found opt-out treatment to be encouraged for hard-to-reach populations.

This study examined the implementation of ChatGPT-assisted Problem-Based Learning (PBL) with a Deep Learning approach in global warming instruction and analyzed changes in students’ scientific literacy before and after the intervention. A pre-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design was used with 30 students in Class X-1 at SMA Negeri 5 Kota Serang during the 2025/2026 academic year. The research instruments consisted of instructional materials, a 22-item scientific literacy test that had passed content and empirical validation, and an observation sheet. Descriptive statistics and a paired-sample t-test were used to analyze the test data, while observation data were summarized as percentages across scientific knowledge, context, science competencies, and science identity. The mean scientific literacy score increased from 76.36 on the pretest to 85.60 on the posttest, and the paired-sample t-test showed a statistically significant difference, t(29) = -6.925, p < .001. Observation results also showed higher percentages in all four scientific literacy aspects during the second learning session. These findings indicate positive changes in students’ scientific literacy following the intervention; however, because the study did not include a comparison group, the changes cannot be attributed exclusively to the intervention.

This chapter operationalizes the concept of trustworthy Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science by translating ethical principles into concrete technical, organizational, and governance requirements for high-risk sporting contexts. It identifies seven core dimensions of trustworthy AI—human agency and oversight, technical robustness, privacy and data governance, transparency, fairness, societal well-being, and accountability—and examines their specific implications for sport environments characterized by physical risk, power asymmetries, and career-defining decisions. The chapter further explores potential risks arising from the misuse or incomplete implementation of these principles, including athlete surveillance, hidden algorithmic decision-making, and deterministic scoring systems that may negatively influence career trajectories. In response, it introduces the Fair Play AI Framework, a sport-specific governance model structured around the PLAY acronym: Procedural Fairness, Lifecycle Autonomy, Authority and Accountability, and Yield to Context. This framework integrates explainability, contestability, contextual validation, and human oversight into a coherent decision-support architecture. By linking ethical theory, regulatory considerations, and applied sport practice, the chapter provides a structured approach for implementing responsible AI systems that enhance performance and health outcomes while preserving athlete autonomy, fairness, and institutional accountability in Sports Science.

documents.abstract: This community service program was conducted to improve teachers' competence in designing Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted learning media at Yayasan Rahmat Islamiyah, Medan. The program was motivated by the gap between the rapid development of AI-based educational technology and the limited digital pedagogical capacity of teachers in many Islamic educational foundations, which still rely on conventional, text-based teaching media. Teachers at the foundation faced difficulties in producing communicative visual, audio-visual, presentation, and video-based learning media, as well as in building effective communication with young learners. The program was carried out through four stages adapted from the management cycle of planning, organizing, actuating, and controlling, followed by an evaluation stage using Kirkpatrick's four-level model. Activities included lectures, hands-on workshops, mentoring, and simulation of AI tool usage such as Canva AI, CapCut AI, and presentation-generation platforms, grounded in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework. Results show a significant increase in teachers' knowledge and skills, reflected in pre-test and post-test scores, active participation, and the production of AI-assisted teaching media by all participants. Teachers also reported improved confidence in communicating with children through more engaging, visualized instructional content. This PKM concludes that structured, AI-based media-design training effectively strengthens teacher competence and can serve as a sustainable model for continuous professional development in Islamic educational foundations facing similar digital transformation challenges.

With the rapid development of live-streaming e-commerce and artificial intelligence, human and AI live-streaming have become two product information disclosure formats in online retail. From the perspective of product information disclosure, we develop a game-theoretic model of a live-streaming e-commerce supply chain comprising a brand owner and an e-commerce platform. We derive Stackelberg equilibria under the resale mode through backward induction, obtain the optimal retail price and information disclosure level under the agency mode through joint optimization, and then compare disclosure-format and sales-mode preferences. The results show that (1) AI live-streaming does not always achieve a higher information disclosure level. It leads to a higher disclosure level only when consumer trust in AI live-streaming disclosure is high, or when trust is moderate and sensitivity to the information disclosure level is low; otherwise, human live-streaming disclosure achieves a higher disclosure level. (2) Under the resale mode, the brand owner and the e-commerce platform have consistent preferences regarding disclosure formats. Both prefer AI live-streaming when consumer trust in AI disclosure is high, or when trust is low but sensitivity is also low, whereas both prefer human live-streaming when trust is low and sensitivity is high. Under the agency mode, their preferences diverge when consumer trust is low and sensitivity is moderate. (3) Regarding sales modes, the brand owner prefers the agency mode only when the commission rate and consumer sensitivity to information disclosure are both low; otherwise, it prefers the resale mode. These findings provide theoretical and managerial implications for disclosure-format selection and sales-mode decisions in live-streaming e-commerce.

documents.abstract: Abstract Kurun (2026) provides a new argument against the possibility of replicating entrepreneurship with AI. The reference is to the socialist calculation debate, where it is contended that AI technology may enable us one day to plan the economy centrally through data analysis and predictive techniques. The paper itself argues that entrepreneurial discovery and, subsequently, innovation and economic evolution cannot be recreated outside of the market, no matter our technological infrastructure, because AI systems are forms of disembodied cognition. Entrepreneurship needs an embodied, situated, and affective perspective. I briefly present the paper’s context and main argument. I wish to apply the paper’s consideration further to show how the creativity of human entrepreneurs cannot be recreated neither by dedicated generative AI models nor by cooperative entrepreneurship. Finally, I highlight the alternative approach to the same conclusion, namely, the ontological strategy, in the different angle and advantages it brings in.

The article examines the impact of the digital educational environment on linguistics, translation studies and foreign language teaching. Particular attention is paid to the use of digital platforms, artificial intelligence, electronic dictionaries, language corpora, machine translation and multimedia resources. Their role in developing students’ communicative, linguistic, translation and digital competences is analysed. In addition, the advantages and limitations of applying digital technologies in the educational process are considered. The importance of integrating innovative tools into foreign language teaching and into the training of future specialists in linguistics and translation is substantiated.

This study aims to examine a structural framework integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Personality Traits into the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) model, with intention acting as a mediating variable on Shariah investment decisions among Generation Z in Indonesia. Data analysis was conducted using a quantitative approach with Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that TPB has a positive and significant effect on investment intention. Intention also strongly mediates the relationship between TPB and investment decisions and has a significant direct impact on actual investment decisions. Conversely, AI and Personality Traits do not significantly influence investment intention, and intention fails to mediate the effect of these variables on investment decisions. The study concludes that for Generation Z investors, external stimuli, social trends, and platform accessibility reflected in the TPB model dominate the decision-making process far more than intrinsic personality factors or pure AI algorithmic features that lack human validation for Shariah compliance. Therefore, the Islamic capital market industry is advised to prioritize the development of social ecosystems and user-friendly application designs.

documents.abstract: Current research remains mostly technocratic and fragmented, neglecting the integration of ethical, spiritual, and revelatory aspects into Islamic educational philosophy, even as artificial intelligence (AI) advances rapidly and transforms the epistemological underpinnings of education. This research reexamines the works of Al-Ghazali and Ibn Rushd, who represent opposing epistemological traditions of spiritual-intuitive and rational-empirical approaches, to create an integrative framework that bridges this gap. Primary writings by scholars, along with current literature on AI and education, serve as the main data sources for this study, which takes a qualitative philosophical-hermeneutic methodology. The research employs comparative and interpretive analysis to examine key themes, including dehumanization, algorithmic bias, and the existential threats posed by AI in educational settings. The research recommends an integrated epistemological framework that methodically integrates revelation (wahy), reason ('aql), and ethical practice (akhlaq) into the learning process. Ethical-spiritual consciousness is presented as the cornerstone of the synthesis, with logical inquiry serving as its operational mechanism within a complementary framework. In the age of artificial intelligence, this leads to a new theoretical framework, "integrative Islamic AI-oriented epistemology," that provides a comprehensive conceptual foundation for developing intellectually sound, morally grounded, and spiritually focused instructional methods. Meskipun kemajuan kecerdasan buatan (AI) sangat cepat dan mengubah dasar pemahaman pendidikan, penelitian yang ada masih cenderung teknis dan terpisah, serta belum menggabungkan aspek etis, spiritual, dan wahyu dalam pendidikan Islam. Untuk mengatasi kekurangan tersebut, penelitian ini mengkaji kembali pemikiran Ibn Rushd dan Al-Ghazali yang mewakili tradisi rasional-empiris dan spiritual-intuitif secara saling melengkapi untuk membangun kerangka pemahaman yang terintegrasi. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan metode filosofis-hermeneutik, dengan sumber data utama adalah karya-karya asli kedua tokoh serta literatur modern tentang AI dan pendidikan. Melalui analisis interpretatif dan perbandingan, penelitian ini meneliti masalah dehumanisasi, bias algoritma, dan tantangan eksistensial dalam pendidikan. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan suatu model epistemologi terintegrasi yang menghubungkan wahyu, akal, dan akhlak secara sistematis dalam proses pembelajaran. Sintesis ini menempatkan kesadaran etis-spiritual sebagai dasar, sementara rasionalitas dan berpikir kritis berfungsi sebagai alat operasional. Temuan ini menghasilkan formulasi teoretis baru yang disebut “epistemologi Islam terintegrasi berbasis AI,” sebagai dasar konseptual untuk pengembangan praktik pendidikan yang cerdas secara intelektual, kuat secara etis, dan mendalam secara spiritual di era kecerdasan buatan.

Cancer is a complex and highly heterogeneous disease driven by intricate molecular interactions across diverse biological processes. Due to this complexity, relying on a single type of biological data—known as a “single-omics” approach—is often insufficient to fully understand how cancer develops or how it may respond to treatment. In this chapter, we present a comprehensive framework for integrating multi-omics data using computational intelligence (CI) approaches to enhance cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutic decision-making. We emphasize the pivotal roles of epigenetic regulation, cellular dynamics, and mitochondrial function, and demonstrate how their complex interplay drives tumor initiation, progression, and treatment response. Furthermore, we explain how artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and network-based methodologies enable the effective integration of high-dimensional omics datasets. These integrated data analyses support the identification of biomarkers, classification of disease subtypes, and discovery of drug response patterns. Special emphasis had been given to the areas like epigenomic modeling (e.g., DNA methylation and histone modification) for early detection; single-cell and spatial transcriptomics to decode the tumor microenvironment and track cell state transitions; and mitochondrial multi-omics to uncover metabolic dependencies and mechanisms of treatment resistance.

A expansão de sistemas de inteligência artificial em cursos a distância reorienta práticas, papéis e decisões de qualidade, com efeitos simultâneos sobre desenho didático, avaliação, ética e gestão acadêmica. O objetivo deste estudo é analisar, a partir de pesquisa bibliográfica, as vantagens, desvantagens e desafios do uso de inteligência artificial em cursos a distância, com foco em implicações pedagógicas, tecnológicas, éticas e de gestão da qualidade. Adotou-se revisão bibliográfica narrativa de publicações entre 2020 e 2025 indexadas na Scientific Electronic Library Online e acessíveis no Portal de Periódicos da CAPES, contemplando ensaios, estudos empíricos e artigos de debate que tratam de inteligência artificial, educação a distância e ensino online. Os achados indicam ganhos potenciais em personalização, apoio à tutoria, feedback imediato e analítica da aprendizagem, com relatos de maior engajamento quando docentes articulam presença pedagógica e desenho com Universal Design for Learning. Em contrapartida, emergem riscos de homogeneização de produções, vigilância excessiva, vieses algorítmicos, plágio via generative AI e dependência instrumental que prejudica autonomia intelectual, além de desafios regulatórios e de governança de qualidade. Conclui-se que a implementação responsável requer critérios de acessibilidade, políticas de transparência, avaliação formativa inclusiva, formação docente contínua e monitoramento institucional de impactos, de modo que benefícios tecnológicos se convertam em aprendizagem significativa e em trajetórias de permanência acadêmica.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This article examines the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into psychiatry, highlighting both its transformative potential and its ethical, clinical, and philosophical challenges. AI applications (ranging from diagnostic algorithms and predictive models to therapeutic chatbots and neuroimplants) are reshaping mental healthcare by improving early detection, personalizing treatments, and expanding access to services, particularly in resource-limited settings. Advanced techniques such as machine learning and natural language processing enable the analysis of multimodal data, enhancing clinical decision-making and enabling preventive interventions. However, the adoption of AI raises significant concerns. These include risks to privacy, algorithmic bias, lack of transparency, and challenges in ensuring informed consent, particularly in vulnerable psychiatric populations. Neurotechnologies such as deep brain stimulation (DBS), especially when assisted by AI, introduce further ethical dilemmas related to autonomy, identity, and long-term safety. The article argues that these challenges cannot be addressed without a deeper conceptual understanding of mental disorders. It advocates for a pluralistic and enactivist framework, which views mental health conditions as dynamic interactions between brain, body, and environment. Ultimately, the responsible integration of AI in psychiatry requires robust ethical governance, interdisciplinary collaboration, and a human-centered approach.

documents.abstract: Traditional machine learning teaching commonly suffers from repetitive experimental paradigms and narrow real-world application contexts, which leads students to rely on mechanical code replication and surface-level learning. This instructional pattern fails to cultivate interdisciplinary cognition and humanistic accomplishment. To improve the current teaching deficiencies, this study adopts digitized Dunhuang mural resources as an innovative teaching medium to develop interdisciplinary practice cases. Following the design concepts of staged ability progression, integration of technical and artistic perspectives, and authentic scenario orientation, this research constructs a three-tier teaching system including basic training, in-depth exploration and comprehensive innovation. The practical curriculum covers a full range of computer vision tasks: Dunhuang image preprocessing, stylistic discrimination, CNN visual recognition, artistic style migration, decorative pattern generation, and damaged mural inpainting. All experimental units combine algorithm engineering practice with Dunhuang art and cultural instruction. This study develops two-dimensional teaching support resources. It also constructs a tailored T-A-P evaluation system that integrates technical ability, artistic attainment and practical performance. The comprehensive student assessment covers coding skills, model error analysis and cultural aesthetic understanding. Classroom teaching practice has proven that the designed case system can significantly strengthen students’ machine learning engineering capabilities and enrich their cultural accomplishment. This research offers a feasible and referable paradigm for interdisciplinary integration in artificial intelligence teaching.

The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education presents both opportunities and challenges for shaping students’ ethical behavior. This study aims to analyze the internalization of moral values in Islamic Religious Education (PAI) as a foundation for developing students’ ethical behavior in the use of AI. Theoretically, this study contributes to the development of Islamic Religious Education and moral education scholarship in responding to technological advancement, while practically providing a foundation for developing AI-oriented ethical learning in PAI. This study employed a qualitative approach with a case study design. Data were collected through in-depth interviews, observations, and documentation and analyzed thematically through coding, categorization, theme identification, and interpretation. The findings indicate that the internalization of moral values occurs through several interconnected stages: value recognition, critical understanding, appreciation, habituation, and actualization. The values of ṣidq (honesty), amanah (trustworthiness), responsibility, tabayyun (verification), respect for others’ work, and self-control constitute important foundations for shaping students’ ethical behavior when using AI. The novelty of this study lies in proposing an akhlaq-based AI literacy perspective, integrating technological literacy with the internalization of Islamic moral values in PAI learning. This perspective positions AI not merely as a learning technology but also as a new context for character formation and ethical development among students.

Digital device use has been associated with cognitive function; however, device ownership and internet search use are often considered together despite potentially differing levels of cognitive engagement. To examine the associations of digital device ownership and internet search use with low cognitive function in community-dwelling older adults. This cross-sectional study included 821 community-dwelling older adults (mean age, 78.4 ± 5.7 years; 91.7% female). Digital device ownership and internet search use were assessed by self-report. Participants were categorized as non-digital device owners, device owners without internet search use, or device owners with internet search use. Cognitive function was assessed using a validated virtual reality-based eye-tracking examination, and low cognitive function was defined as a total score below 75. Logistic regression analyses examined the associations between group membership and low cognitive function after adjustment for age, sex, educational level, living status, polypharmacy, depressive symptoms, hypertension, history of stroke, and history of Parkinson’s disease. The prevalence of low cognitive function was 70.2% among non-digital device owners, 57.8% among device owners without internet search use, and 30.6% among device owners with internet search use. Compared with non-digital device owners, device owners without internet search use did not have significantly different odds of low cognitive function (odds ratio: 0.70; 95% confidence interval: 0.37–1.35; P = .291), whereas device owners with internet search use had significantly lower odds (odds ratio: 0.39; 95% confidence interval: 0.20–0.75; P = .005). Digital device ownership accompanied by internet search use was more strongly associated with lower odds of low cognitive function than ownership alone.

This study evaluates interpretable supervised machine learning for three-class narrative framing classification of literary text, using Mary Shelley's Frankenstein (1818) as a case study; narrative framing is the evaluative position a passage assigns to the Creature: Threat, Victim, or Ambivalent. The methodology comprised five stages: (1) extraction of passages narrated by Victor Frankenstein, the Creature, and Robert Walton from the 1818 Project Gutenberg text; (2) annotation of 195 passages, with a blinded second annotator re-labeling 68 passages (Cohen's κ = 0.6926); (3) sublinear TF-IDF unigram and bigram representation; (4) classification with Multinomial Naive Bayes, Linear SVM, and Logistic Regression against Majority and VADER baselines under stratified 5-fold cross-validation; and (5) a designation-masking ablation and coefficient analysis. The results show that Logistic Regression obtained the highest mean scores (66.67% accuracy; 47.75% Macro-F1), although its margin over Linear SVM (46.18%) and VADER (44.85%) lies within fold-level variability. Pooled F1 reached 69.0% for Threat and 74.3% for Victim, whereas none of the 29 Ambivalent passages was correctly identified. Masking explicit designations reduced Macro-F1 only to 45.20%, indicating partial robustness to this procedure rather than discourse-level modeling. It is concluded that interpretable classical classifiers can separate Threat from Victim framing using transparent lexical evidence but cannot yet detect ambiguous framing; given the single-novel, small, and imbalanced dataset, the findings are a preliminary proof of concept. Future work should enlarge and balance the corpus, apply group-based and repeated cross-validation, and compare context-aware models, including large language models, on the Ambivalent class.

Stability theorems on intersecting families are often formulated via the covering number of set families. Let $M(n,k,t)$ denote the maximum size of a $k$-uniform intersecting family $\mathcal F\subseteq \binom{[n]}{k}$ with covering number $t$. It is known that for any fixed $t$ and fixed $k$ sufficiently large relative to $t$, one has $M(n,k,t)=(p_{t-1}(k)+o(1))(k)\binom{n}{k}$ as $n$ tends to infinity, where $p_{t-1}(k)$ is the maximum number of covers of size $t-1$ that a $k$-uniform intersecting family can have provided its covering number is $t-1$. Frankl, Ota, and Tokushige conjectured that $p_t(k)=k^t-\binom{t}{2}k^{t-1}+O_t(k^{t-2})$ for fixed $t$ as $k$ tends to infinity and they also showed that $p_t(k)=k^t-b(t)k^{t-1}+O_t(k^{t-2})$, where $b(t)$ is defined as the extremum of the following minimization problem. Suppose a $k$-uniform intersecting family $\mathcal F$ of covering number $t$ can be partitioned into $\mathcal F_1,\dots,\mathcal F_t$ such that for every $i$ there exists a set $X_i$ with $X_i \subseteq F_i$ for all $F_i\in\mathcal F_i$ and the $X_i$'s are pairwise disjoint and non-empty. Then $b(t)$ is the minimum of $\sum_{i=1}^t(k-|X_i|)$ over all such families, partitions and $X_i$'s. In accordance with the conjecture on $p_t(k)$, Frankl, Ota, and Tokushige conjectured $b(t)=\binom{t}{2}$ for all $t\ge 2$ and proved $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\lfloor \frac{t-1}{2}\rfloor^{3/2}\le b(t)\le \binom{t}{2}$. In this note, we present a counterexample to the conjecture showing $b(t)\le 2\sqrt2\,t^{3/2}\sqrt{\log t}$ $+O(t^{3/2})$ and improve the lower bound to $\frac{2}{3^{3/4}}t^{3/2}-O(t)\le b(t)$. The counterexample was found by ChatGPT 6.1Sol, the lower bound proof is due to the human author.

documents.abstract: Interactive webpages underpin modern applications, but reproducing both their visual appearance and multi-step behavior remains challenging for multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Scalable training data must capture user actions, state transitions, and expected outcomes, while real-world webpage code is often entangled with irrelevant scripts and external dependencies. Moreover, existing GUI-agent-based verification provides slow and potentially unstable functional feedback. To address these challenges, we propose InterWebCoder, an efficient framework for interactive webpage code generation. InterWebCoder introduces a Test-Specification-Guided and Execution-Verified Data Synthesis pipeline that records real-world interaction trajectories and synthesizes self-contained webpage code with executable test scripts. A failureattributed repair mechanism uses runtime evidence to locate and iteratively fix errors in either the webpage code or test script. We then combine test-ID-weighted supervised fine-tuning with group-relative policy optimization, directly optimizing functional correctness and visual fidelity using test pass rates and state-level visual similarity. This replaces costly GUI-agent verification with fast, reproducible executable feedback. Our pipeline produces 1,736 verified samples from 2,058 tasks, achieving an 84.35% synthesis success rate. On IWR-Bench and Vision2Web, InterWebCoder achieves final scores of 48.54 and 48.42 with a 9B backbone, outperforming 30B-level models and Gemini-3.7-Flash while remaining competitive with Claude-Sonnet-5. It reduces reward-computation latency by over 97%, eliminates external MLLM verification costs, and accelerates end-to-end training by up to 1.4x.

Abstract This introductory chapter has three sections. Section 1.1, begins by explaining the concept of welfare. In short, AIs have welfare just in case they are worthy of a certain distinctive kind of moral consideration. Then, it surveys the leading theories of welfare, which claim that welfare consists in pleasure, or satisfied desire, or participation in what is objectively good. It argues that these theories agree that whether AIs have welfare depends on three factors: agency, consciousness, and sentience. Section 1.2 reflects on methodology. The arguments in subsequent chapters presuppose functionalism, which understands mental states in terms of complex patterns of causation. The book also adopts a top-down methodology, which applies existing philosophical theories of agency, consciousness, and sentience to AIs. Section 1.3 introduces the AIs discussed in the book: large language models, language model agents, and reinforcement learners.

documents.abstract: This chapter introduces artificial intelligence as an economic phenomenon rather than as a purely technical achievement. It defines AI, in the language of economics, as a family of technologies that lowers the cost of prediction, pattern recognition, classification, content generation, and increasingly decision support. The chapter explains why this cost shock matters for productivity, labor demand, inequality, market structure, state capacity, and global development. It also situates AI within the longer history of general-purpose technologies such as steam, electricity, and information technology, while emphasizing the distinctive feature of contemporary AI: its ability to enter non-routine cognitive tasks previously protected from automation. The chapter presents the organizing framework of the book. AI does not simply “replace jobs” or “create growth”. It reallocates tasks, changes complementarities between humans and capital, alters firm boundaries, and forces governments to rethink taxation, regulation, education, and social insurance. The chapter concludes with a roadmap for the remaining chapters.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: This chapter introduces the concept of Artificial Intelligence in Sports Science and situates it within the broader transformation of sport into a data-driven and analytically intensive domain. It argues that Artificial Intelligence has evolved from a supportive computational tool into an active component of decision-making processes in performance optimization, injury prevention, training design, and sport management. The chapter traces the historical and conceptual origins of Artificial Intelligence, from early philosophical reflections and mechanical prototypes to the emergence of modern data-intensive systems enabled by advances in computational power and large-scale data availability. Building on this context, the chapter establishes sport as an ideal empirical environment for AI applications due to its structured rules, measurable outcomes, and continuous data generation. It introduces key methodological paradigms, particularly supervised learning and unsupervised learning, and explains their complementary roles in predictive modeling and pattern discovery within sports analytics. By integrating historical perspective, conceptual clarification, and methodological foundations, this chapter provides a structured entry point into machine learning, data-driven analysis, and performance modelling in sport, forming the theoretical basis for subsequent chapters focused on neural networks, Bayesian inference, and advanced AI applications in Sports Science.

This article presents the fundamental foundations and specific characteristics of intuition, as well as the mechanisms for its comprehension, particularly within the framework of cybernetics and complex systems theory. Today, intuition is understood in science as a multi-level and complex phenomenon, the process of cognition of which includes both rational and irrational components. The authors convincingly argue that intuition has its own structure and a certain logic; it can be considered within the framework of nonlinear dynamics as a self-organizing system with feedback and multiple mechanisms. The analysis shows that intuitive knowledge arises where research encounters high rates of change not only in the environment but also in its component parts, incomplete empirical data, and a lack of resources. As is well known, the concept of “observer” is introduced within the paradigm of post-non-classical science, particularly within the context of the evolutionary-constructive model of scientific knowledge development. Now the observer is directly viewed as part of the system, and their intuitive decisions are perceived as the result of the interaction of internal cognitive structures with external information flows. As a result, it becomes possible to interpret intuition as a significant factor in cognition, capable of minimizing the tacitness and uncertainty of knowledge. Thus, intuition becomes a natural and objective regulator of the formation of new knowledge through the synthesis of heterogeneous information. Intuition and its mechanisms are well suited to the theory of complex systems. In particular, the phenomenon of self-organization, especially emergence in intuition, is a nonlinear interaction between system elements, resulting in transitions between different cognitive states and the formation of qualitatively new types of knowledge. Research demonstrates how and by what means parallels arise between human intuition and constructed models, how weak and implicit signals are recognized, and how intuitive probabilistic predictions are formed. Conclusion: Intuition is a unique phenomenon, a special adaptive mechanism for knowledge processing, essential for the successful functioning of humans and intelligent systems in the context of the nonequilibrium of the modern world and the increasing complexity of cognitive processes, encompassing both physical reality and the metaphysics of existence. This approach offers new prospects for the development of hybrid human-machine systems, where intuitive and rational mechanisms interact as complementary modes of cognition.

Evaluations of large language model (LLM) agents report that pricing agents collude at others' expense. Yet collusion is defined by enforcement: a cartel, in which competitors share monopoly profits, holds only if a member who cheats is punished. We introduce an audit that tests enforcement by forcing a member to cheat in counterfactual copies of a market, and use it to study what reinforcement learning (RL) teaches agents in pricing and trading. Small LLMs trained by RL learn what their training rivals reward, but only what they readily try. In self-play, they learn fixed rules ignoring their rivals; against a punishing rival, to be deterred; against a cheating rival, to match its cuts, never the costly price war that would deter it, which they rarely try. A war forced into training is learned, but mostly only where it was forced. Against their own copies, deterred and matching agents can earn the same cartel profits, but only matching ones can enforce them, and then thinly: as a by-product and only against large cuts. Q-learners enforce collusion only in pricing. Prompted LLMs reach cartel-like outcomes mostly through rules that ignore the market. Outcome measures cannot tell these cases apart; the audit can.

In-context reinforcement learning (ICRL) exploits the impressive in-context learning ability of large language models to zero-shot generalize to new, unseen tasks at inference time without any parameter updates. Among many approaches, the Decision-Pretrained Transformer (DPT) is particularly appealing for its theoretical grounding: under idealized assumptions such as a sufficiently expressive model and infinite pretraining data, DPT can perform Bayesian posterior sampling. Whether this characterization survives in practice remains open. Therefore, we ask: \textit{is ICRL, specifically DPT and our proposed DPT variants, a Bayesian posterior sampler in practice?} To approach this question, we establish two necessary conditions that a Bayesian posterior sampler must satisfy: \textit{sufficient-statistic invariance} and the \textit{martingale property}. We then construct statistical hypothesis tests to statistically assess if practically-trained ICRL models satisfy these conditions. Applying these tests in Gaussian, Bernoulli, and linear bandit settings, we find that both conditions are consistently violated, suggesting that ICRL may not behave as Bayesian posterior samplers in practice. Beyond this negative result, our tests provide a principled toolkit for testing the Bayesian behavior of ICRL.

The Physical Limit of Capital: Energy, Infrastructure and Geopolitics in the New Resource Economy ISHEA Premiere Report · Vol. 1, No. 1 · September 2026 This report examines the relationship between financial capital, physical resource availability, infrastructure resilience, and geopolitical risk in the global economy. It explores how the expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure, the reconfiguration of energy and mineral supply chains, and the strategic transformation of maritime and logistics corridors are reshaping the conditions under which financial value can be converted into realizable economic activity. Using an interdisciplinary analytical framework informed by biophysical accounting, bioenergetics, cognitive economics, complex systems, and resilience analysis, the report examines three interconnected dimensions: the physical infrastructure supporting AI-related investment; the strategic role of energy resources and logistics corridors in international capital allocation; and the implications of geopolitical disruption for asset valuation and business planning. The report introduces an ISHEA analytical heuristic, Realizable Value, which considers financial value alongside physical availability, logistical resilience, and flow security. This formulation is presented as a diagnostic framework rather than a calibrated or empirically validated valuation model. The report concludes with practical recommendations for business planning in 2026–2027, including physical-dependency audits, geographic and supplier redundancy, energy-risk assessment, and systemic stress testing. Purpose: To contribute to interdisciplinary discussion on the relationship between financial valuation and the physical, infrastructural, and geopolitical conditions that sustain economic activity. Author: Carlos J. Pérez Pulido Institution: ISHEA Institute — International System for Human–Ecological Advancement Keywords: Biophysical economics; financial capital; energy systems; artificial intelligence infrastructure; critical minerals; geopolitical risk; supply-chain resilience; infrastructure security; systemic risk; Economy 5.0. FAIR-DANCE is a scoping review of judging reliability, scoring validity, contextual effects, judge performance, and technology-assisted performance evaluation in DanceSport and other judged sports. This OSF project hosts the review protocol, search documentation, screening and retrieval records, final data-charting dataset, supplementary materials, reporting checklists, methodological amendments, and reproducibility materials. The review maps evidence on reliability and agreement, scoring accuracy and validity, contextual bias, anomalous scoring behaviour, judge education and calibration, competition monitoring and evaluation procedures, digital systems, statistical analytics, and artificial intelligence-supported assessment, with particular emphasis on the potential transferability of these approaches to DanceSport. The review was conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute methodological guidance for scoping reviews and is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Original searches were conducted in Scopus, SPORTDiscus, and PubMed/MEDLINE. A targeted supplementary Scopus sensitivity search conducted on 6 October 2026 identified 10 additional eligible studies, yielding a final analytic corpus of 123 studies. The final synthesis is organised around five complementary dimensions: Measurement Quality, Contextual Fairness, Scoring Monitoring and Anomaly Detection, Technology-Assisted Evaluation, and Evaluation Procedures and Feedback. Continuous judge education and calibration and human-in-the-loop technology are treated as cross-cutting mechanisms supporting technical performance evaluation. Post-registration methodological amendments, supplementary-search decisions, and the complete reproducibility audit trail are documented transparently in this project.

Latar belakang: Kecerdasan Buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) telah mengubah paradigma interpretasi gambar radiologi secara fundamental. Kemampuan deep learning dan machine learning membuka peluang peningkatan akurasi diagnostik, efisiensi waktu pembacaan, dan pengurangan variabilitas antar-pembaca. Namun, bukti komprehensif mengenai dampak AI terhadap berbagai modalitas pencitraan medis masih perlu disintesis secara sistematis. Tujuan: Melakukan tinjauan literatur sistematis (SLR) untuk mensintesis bukti ilmiah mengenai dampak AI terhadap akurasi diagnostik, waktu interpretasi, kepercayaan diagnostik, dan faktor-faktor yang memengaruhi interaksi manusia-AI dalam interpretasi radiologi. Metode: Penelitian ini menggunakan metode SLR mengacu pada panduan PRISMA 2020. Pencarian dilakukan pada PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, dan IEEE Xplore (2021–2025). Dari 847 artikel teridentifikasi, 9 memenuhi kriteria inklusi. Hasil: Sembilan studi mencakup mamografi, rontgen dada, CT scan, MRI, angiografi, dan radiografi muskuloskeletal dengan lebih dari 100.000 kasus. AI meningkatkan sensitivitas diagnostik rata-rata 11,4–23,0%, memperpendek waktu pembacaan kasus normal (rerata 13,3 vs 14,8 detik), dan meningkatkan kepercayaan diagnostik. Kesimpulan: AI terbukti konsisten meningkatkan performa diagnostik radiologi tanpa mengurangi produktivitas.

documents.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi digital dan kecerdasan buatan (Artificial Intelligence/AI) telah membuka peluang baru dalam dunia pendidikan, khususnya dalam pengembangan kreativitas dan literasi digital peserta didik. Namun, masih banyak siswa yang belum mampu memanfaatkan teknologi desain digital secara optimal untuk mendukung kegiatan pembelajaran dan pengabdian kepada masyarakat. Oleh karena itu, kegiatan Pengabdian kepada Masyarakat (PkM) ini bertujuan meningkatkan pemahaman, keterampilan, dan kesiapan siswa dalam menggunakan aplikasi Canva berbasis AI melalui program Pelatihan Kelas Kreatif AI Canva bagi siswa PKM SMAN 1 Lebak Wangi. Metode pelaksanaan kegiatan meliputi ceramah, demonstrasi, praktik langsung (learning by doing), diskusi, pendampingan, dan evaluasi. Keberhasilan program diukur melalui beberapa indikator, yaitu pemahaman materi, kemudahan penggunaan Canva, proses pembuatan desain, kualitas konten, pembelajaran, kolaborasi, fasilitasi, etika dan literasi digital, serta niat menggunakan Canva. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa pelatihan memberikan dampak positif yang signifikan dengan rata-rata capaian sebesar 81,4%, melampaui target yang ditetapkan sebesar 75%. Peningkatan tertinggi terjadi pada indikator kemudahan penggunaan Canva dan niat menggunakan Canva yang masing-masing mencapai 100%, menunjukkan tingginya penerimaan dan motivasi siswa dalam memanfaatkan teknologi AI. Selain itu, peserta berhasil menghasilkan berbagai karya digital berupa poster, infografis, dan media presentasi yang kreatif serta komunikatif. Kegiatan ini membuktikan bahwa pelatihan Canva berbasis AI efektif dalam meningkatkan literasi digital, kreativitas, dan keterampilan desain visual siswa. Program ini juga berkontribusi dalam mempersiapkan generasi muda yang adaptif, inovatif, dan siap menghadapi tantangan transformasi digital di era Society 5.0.

WHEN A CIVILIZATION NO LONGER KNOWS WHERE TO PLACE ITS PEOPLE A BIT Essay on Education, Work, Human Value, and the Finite Human Life Cycle Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This interdisciplinary social and philosophical essay examines a growing concern in modern civilization: the potential disconnection between human educational achievement, accumulated capabilities, labor-market structures, and meaningful participation in society. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay begins with a reported case of a highly educated individual experiencing prolonged difficulty entering stable employment. Rather than interpreting an individual case as evidence of universal labor-market failure, the essay investigates the structural interfaces between education, professional training, recruitment, technological change, and the finite human life cycle. A central argument is that education, businesses, technological systems, and public institutions often operate on different timescales. Education may require many years. Recruitment decisions may be made within months. Technologies can transform occupations rapidly, while human lives continue through irreversible biological and social stages. When these systems become misaligned, the costs of institutional mismatch may be transferred disproportionately to individuals. The essay introduces a BIT interpretation of historical outcomes (Quả lịch sử), emphasizing that a person's abilities and achievements represent accumulated life histories rather than isolated qualifications or current employment status. It discusses the compression of human capabilities into résumés, the disappearance of entry-level opportunities, unused professional knowledge, and the potential loss of social participation when qualified individuals cannot find meaningful opportunities to contribute. The essay proposes examining the transition between education and employment as an important form of social infrastructure. Possible responses include professional transition pathways, mentorship, supervised work opportunities, recognition of transferable capabilities, and institutions capable of connecting human knowledge with real societal needs. Central Proposition A civilization should not be evaluated only by how many people it educates, but also by its ability to transform their accumulated knowledge and capabilities into meaningful participation in collective life. Scope and Limitations This publication is a social and philosophical thought essay, not an empirical demonstration that higher education has lost its value or that artificial intelligence is the cause of unemployment. It does not treat a single reported employment case as representative of the entire labor market. Its purpose is to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about education, employment, human dignity, institutional responsibility, and the preservation of human potential throughout finite life cycles. The original Vietnamese essay references reporting from The Wall Street Journal and materials from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, and the National Science Foundation's National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics. When the Collective Foundation Changes Rhythm A Conditional Foresight Essay on Children, Digital Environments, and the New Historical Outcomes of Humanity Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores how changes in modern environments may influence the formation, transmission, and transformation of collective behavioral foundations across generations. Developed from Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Source Ontology Framework 03, the essay examines the relationship between intrinsic human characteristics, historical collective foundations, environmental change, and emerging technological systems. The central question concerns what may happen when the environments shaping human development change much faster than the biological and structural characteristics of human beings. The essay explores nine conditional future perspectives, including: The increasing difference between long-term intrinsic human characteristics and rapidly changing environments. Digital screens and online interactions becoming major channels through which children acquire and retain experiences. Changes in the relative influence of families, schools, digital platforms, and artificial intelligence on childhood development. Individuals participating simultaneously in multiple overlapping historical and cultural collective foundations. Artificial intelligence becoming an active component in cycles of information retention, behavioral feedback, and social interaction. The growing difficulty of separating intrinsic tendencies from environmentally acquired behavior. Educational approaches moving beyond immediate measurable outcomes toward the design of developmental environments. Societies recognizing how their institutions, technologies, and daily practices shape the foundations inherited by future generations. The possibility of multiple future developmental trajectories rather than one predetermined collective destiny. The BIT cycle Tính – Lưu – Hành – Quả – Tính serves as a conceptual framework for considering how environmental interactions become retained patterns and how present outcomes influence subsequent generations. A central idea is that every generation inherits not only an existing world but also historically established rhythms, practices, expectations, and systems of interaction. Through its activities, each generation may preserve, transform, or replace parts of these inherited foundations. The essay does not assume that digital technology is universally beneficial or harmful. Its potential effects depend on technological design, family environments, education, communities, institutions, and the specific histories of different societies. Scientific scope and limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an experimentally validated theory of human development. It does not predict that collective human behavior must follow a single technological, social, or historical trajectory. The proposed perspectives are intended to encourage interdisciplinary discussion about childhood, education, technological environments, human adaptability, artificial intelligence, and responsibility toward future generations. WHEN A DEGREE IS NO LONGER A PROMISE A Conditional Foresight Essay on Education, Employment, and Human Life-Cycle Transition Infrastructure Author: Bùi Quang TrịnhIndependent Researcher, VietnamFounder, Boundary Information Theory (BIT) Abstract This conditional foresight essay explores possible transformations in education, employment, professional identity, and social institutions as artificial intelligence, automation, and rapidly changing economic structures reshape the relationship between human knowledge and work. Developed within the Boundary Information Theory (BIT) research programme, the essay asks whether future civilization will be able to maintain meaningful transitions between learning, professional contribution, personal development, and a dignified human life. The essay presents nine conditional future perspectives. First, academic degrees may increasingly function as evidence of educational achievement rather than implicit guarantees of specific professional positions. Second, automation and artificial intelligence may reduce certain entry-level tasks, potentially weakening traditional pathways through which younger generations acquire professional experience. Third, institutions may develop transferable capability profiles that recognize practical skills, interdisciplinary competence, and demonstrated problem-solving ability beyond conventional occupational titles. Fourth, universities may expand their responsibilities by supporting graduates through longer professional transitions rather than ending institutional support at graduation. Fifth, countries may begin treating unused human expertise as a potential public resource, creating mechanisms to connect available capabilities with unmet social needs. Sixth, careers may increasingly involve multiple transitions among employment, education, independent work, care responsibilities, and periods of recovery. Seventh, artificial intelligence may improve labor-market matching while simultaneously creating new risks of algorithmic exclusion, opacity, and unfair screening. Eighth, future institutions may recognize periods of unemployment, retraining, caregiving, and independent research as legitimate phases of human development rather than treating them as personal deficiencies. Ninth, the evaluation of education and employment policies may shift toward their long-term effects on the complete human life cycle, including health, family formation, professional resilience, social participation, and security in later life. Central Proposition The future value of education may depend not only on academic credentials, but also on whether civilization develops effective bridges between human learning, meaningful contribution, and dignified life transitions. The essay suggests that education, employers, governments, and technological systems may need to share responsibility for maintaining these pathways. Scope and Limitations This publication is a conditional foresight essay, not a probabilistic forecast or an empirically established prediction. It does not claim that academic degrees will necessarily lose their value, that artificial intelligence will inevitably eliminate entry-level employment, or that one institutional model will suit every society. The possibilities discussed may emerge differently across countries, economic sectors, and social groups. The purpose is to contribute to public reflection and interdisciplinary research on education, artificial intelligence, employment transitions, institutional design, and human-centered civilization. Language-model agents are being proposed to investigate fraud and money-laundering alerts under selective autonomy: the agent closes some cases itself and escalates the rest to a human analyst. Which cases it escalates determines the division of labor, the analysts' workload, and the errors that reach customers and regulators, yet the knowledge needed to design that rule is divided among learning to defer and selective prediction, uncertainty estimation for language models, and research on human reliance on AI advice. This survey connects the three through the escalation loop of a fraud-investigation team and restates known results from these literatures in one notation. We state the cost-optimal escalation rule, which requires different confidence thresholds for closing a case as benign and for concluding fraud, and its form under a fixed analyst capacity; show that calibration suffices for selective risk to be monotone and interpretable; state the conformal bound on the rate of cases that are both closed automatically and wrong; show when combining uncertainty signals helps and when correlated signals double-count; show that the error among automatically closed cases is not identified without audits and is estimable with them; and quantify how analyst reliance on the agent's verdict erodes the value of escalation. Against this basis we compare deferral rules and uncertainty signals, and conclude that threshold-based deferral rules assume a calibrated confidence that agents do not yet provide, that agent-level uncertainty estimation is only beginning, and that, to our knowledge, no peer-reviewed study has yet evaluated an escalation rule for a fraud-investigation agent together with the analysts who receive its cases.

documents.abstract: For millennia, knowledge has been carried by language, and large language models still put language at the center. Yet the coding agents built on these models mostly write code. This paper is a contribution to epistemology, which asks what kind of knowledge code is and how it is obtained. We define knowledge as code as knowledge written in a programming language or in a machine-parsable data format, whose validity can be checked by executing it. We define thirteen epistemic properties of knowledge media and show that code is the first medium to have all of them. We distinguish two ways in which knowledge enters code, encoding and learning by execution, where code is both the experiment and the record of its result. Agents make learning by execution observable, since their trajectories record every probe, observation and line of code they keep. Code is thus not only a tool of knowledge work but a knowledge medium in its own right, the first that can check what it holds.

Various voices warn of the growing anti-humanism that prevails today. This risk of the devaluation of humanity finds a salient example—in the context of posthumanism in its cybernetic form—in the unstoppable development of AI with the emergence of products such as ChatGPT, capable of generating literary, musical, or pictorial compositions. This is a technology that enables humans to delegate to non-thinking machines the responsibility for the task of thinking in its different domains—cognitive, evaluative, or artistic creation— thus running the risk of falling back, in Kantian terms, into a condition of immaturity. The task of thought—and, therefore, of philosophy—should consist in remaining vigilant in order to resist such temptations and, if possible, in exercising with greater firmness that faculty of thinking characteristic of humans, by analyzing the age in which they find themselves and the dangers that lie in wait for them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) changes labor markets and the distribution of income. It begins by distinguishing skill-biased, routine-biased, and task-biased technological change, then explains why generative AI requires a further shift in emphasis from occupations to tasks, workflows, and organizational control. The chapter argues that AI affects inequality through several channels at once: direct task displacement, productivity gains, the creation of new tasks, changes in market power, and differences in worker bargaining power. A central claim is that exposure to AI is not the same as technological unemployment. The distributional consequences depend on adoption costs, complementary investments, institutions, and the allocation of productivity rents inside firms and across markets. This chapter, therefore, treats AI neither as an automatic engine of mass unemployment nor as a neutral productivity tool, but as a general-purpose technology whose labor market effects are mediated by economic structure and policy.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Although large language models (LLMs) encode language in highly distributed spaces, they remain vulnerable to focal disruptions---a phenomenon strikingly similar to how localized brain damage causes clinical aphasia in humans. To investigate this theoretical tension, we ask whether LLMs possess a functional structure analogous to the human language system, by introducing a novel mechanistic interpretability framework inspired by aphasia. Through two complementary approaches, classifier-guided lesioning and continuous activation steering, we systematically induce aphasia-like breakdowns in LLMs. We find that language functions can be successfully isolated to discrete structural circuits and continuous representational vectors, yet these functions remain densely entangled with significant circuit overlap and vector similarities across distinct aphasic profiles. Furthermore, while steering generalizes robustly across downstream tasks, structural lesioning remains asymmetrically constrained. By bridging neuropsychology and mechanistic interpretability, we demonstrate that LLMs, functionally analogous to biological brains, rely on a densely entangled architecture that can be systematically mapped through clinically-informed interventions.

Highway ramp merging is a safety-critical interaction for automated-vehicle validation because gap acceptance, longitudinal control, and lane-changing responses are coupled within a short time horizon. This paper presents a rule-distillation framework in which a large language model (LLM) serves only as an offline calibrator of a compact, interpretable rule expert: the model receives scalar replay statistics and proposes bounded updates of three rule parameters, every candidate is verified by closed-loop simulation, and the accepted rule expert is re-executed under legal-action masking and safety filtering to produce feasible demonstrations for an adversarial ramp actor, which is then fine-tuned by multi-agent reinforcement learning on a fixed scenario-replay library. On the training-distribution library, the distilled adversary reaches the highest evaluation return and reward-collision rate of the three schemes. This advantage only partly carries over to 150 held-out scenarios, where its reward-collision rate becomes indistinguishable from that of training from scratch (42.7% against 40.7%, overlapping intervals) while its evaluation return and its rate of successfully induced evasive responses remain higher. Against random-search and Bayesian-optimization calibrators evaluated under the same parameter ranges, score and simulation budget, the LLM attains a comparable calibration score with roughly one third of the closed-loop simulations and with a smaller run-to-run spread, but it is not a better global optimizer at the full budget, so it is best characterized as a sample-efficient and low-variance calibrator. The results indicate that verified rule calibration provides effective initialization for adversarial reinforcement learning within the evaluated simulation setting.

Objective This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI anxiety among medical imaging students and to examine the associations of emotional flexibility, future employment anxiety, and demographic variables with profile membership, thereby providing empirical evidence for differentiated psychological intervention strategies. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted using convenience sampling among 488 medical imaging students recruited from North Sichuan Medical College in Sichuan Province, China. Data were collected using the AI Anxiety Scale, the Emotional Flexibility Scale, the Future Employment Anxiety Scale, and a demographic questionnaire. Latent profile analysis was used to identify AI anxiety profiles, and the three-step BCH and R3STEP procedures were used to examine distal outcomes and covariates while accounting for classification uncertainty. Results Latent profile analysis identified three severity-ordered AI anxiety profiles: a Medium AI anxiety profile (65.78%), a High AI anxiety profile (22.75%), and a Low AI anxiety profile (11.48%). The High profile scored most prominently on Job Replacement and Sociotechnical Blindness anxiety. Emotional flexibility showed a nonlinear distribution across profiles: highest in the Low profile (BCH M = 3.975), lowest in the Medium profile (3.282), and intermediate in the High profile (3.805). Future employment anxiety increased monotonically across the profiles (Low: 2.285; Medium: 3.255; High: 4.126; all pairwise p < 0.001) and independently distinguished all profiles in the classification-error-adjusted (R3STEP) analysis. Emotional flexibility was lowest in the Medium profile and did not differ between the High and Low profiles ( p = 0.271); in the classification-error-adjusted analysis, it distinguished the High from the Medium profile but not the Low from the Medium profile. Conclusion The findings support differentiated psychological support tailored to distinct AI anxiety profiles, and suggest that AI literacy education and career planning guidance should be systematically integrated into medical imaging curricula.
